reviewNote: Demo content written for the Inama MVP. It must be reviewed and validated by RAB agronomists before real farmers rely on it.

stageTips.title: Check your maize for armyworm
stageTips.body: Young maize is hit hardest by fall armyworm. Walk your field in a W and look closely at 20 plants.

stageTips.title: Top-dress maize when it is knee-high
stageTips.body: Maize needs nitrogen most at knee height. Put a small pinch of urea in a ring a hand-width from each plant, then cover it with soil.

stageTips.title: Dry maize well before storing
stageTips.body: Dry cobs until a grain cracks when you bite it, then store in airtight bags off the floor.

stageTips.title: Weed your beans early
stageTips.body: Weeds take the water and food your beans need. Weed before flowering, when the soil is not wet.

stageTips.title: Look under bean leaves for rust
stageTips.body: Rusty powder under the leaves means bean rust. Check a few plants each week after rain.

stageTips.title: Check cassava leaves for disease
stageTips.body: Look for mosaic patterns, brown spots or drying shoots. Pull out sick plants early so disease does not spread.

stageTips.title: Watch potatoes for late blight after rain
stageTips.body: Cool, wet weather brings late blight fast. Check leaves for dark, wet-looking patches.

stageTips.title: Watch bananas for wilt
stageTips.body: Yellow, wilting leaves and early-ripening fruit can mean banana wilt. Clean tools between plants.

stageTips.title: Hill up sweet potato soil
stageTips.body: Cover cracks in the soil around roots to keep weevils out.

stageTips.title: Check rice for blast
stageTips.body: Diamond-shaped spots with grey centres are rice blast. Check after cool, wet nights.

stageTips.title: Look under coffee leaves for rust
stageTips.body: Orange powder under the leaves is coffee leaf rust. Prune for airflow and remove fallen leaves.

stageTips.title: Pull out striga before it flowers
stageTips.body: Striga steals water and food from sorghum. Pull it by hand before it seeds.

stageTips.title: Check tomato leaves for leaf miner
stageTips.body: Winding trails inside leaves mean Tuta absoluta. Remove affected leaves early.

conditions.name: Fall armyworm
conditions.headline: Your maize may have fall armyworm
signs: Small “windows” or ragged holes in young leaves
Sawdust-like droppings in the funnel
Caterpillars hiding in the funnel
conditions.notSeenHint: A pale Y shape on the caterpillar’s head — look closely
conditions.whatsHappening: Fall armyworm caterpillars are feeding inside the funnel of your maize.
conditions.whyItMatters: Young maize can lose its growing point in a few days, and the caterpillars move from plant to plant.
steps: Walk your field in a W and look closely at 20 plants.
Crush egg clusters and small caterpillars by hand.
Put a pinch of dry soil or ash into each damaged funnel.

If 4 or more of the 20 plants have fresh damage: If you must spray, use only a product on RAB’s approved list from a registered agro-dealer. Follow the label, wear gloves and a mask, and keep children away.
Check again in 3 days.
sources: FAO guidance on fall armyworm management
Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Maize lethal necrosis
conditions.headline: Your maize may have maize lethal necrosis
signs: Yellowing that starts at the leaf edges
Leaves drying from the edges inwards
Plants stay small
conditions.notSeenHint: Rotten cobs with few grains — check the ears
conditions.whatsHappening: A virus disease is making the leaves yellow and dry from the edges.
conditions.whyItMatters: It spreads through insects and infected seed, and badly affected plants give no harvest.
steps: Pull out affected plants and bury or burn them away from the field.
Do not plant maize again in this field next season — rotate with beans.
Use certified seed from a registered agro-dealer.
Tell your farmer promoter so neighbours can check their fields.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Northern leaf blight
conditions.headline: Your maize may have northern leaf blight
signs: Long, cigar-shaped grey-brown streaks
Streaks start on the lower leaves
conditions.notSeenHint: Dark mould inside the streaks in wet weather
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is making long grey-brown streaks on the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: If it reaches the upper leaves before the cobs fill, your harvest will be smaller.
steps: Keep checking the upper leaves each week.
After harvest, remove or bury maize stalks.
Next season, rotate with beans and choose a tolerant variety.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Maize streak virus
conditions.headline: Your maize may have maize streak virus
signs: Thin yellow streaks along the leaf veins
Young plants stay small
conditions.whatsHappening: A virus spread by leafhoppers is making yellow streaks on the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: Plants infected when young often give very small cobs.
steps: Pull out badly affected young plants.
Keep the field free of grassy weeds where leafhoppers live.
Next season, plant early and use a resistant variety.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Nitrogen shortage
conditions.headline: Your maize may be short of nitrogen
signs: Yellowing that starts on the lower, older leaves
A yellow V shape from the leaf tip
conditions.whatsHappening: Your maize is not getting enough nitrogen from the soil.
conditions.whyItMatters: Nitrogen is what makes maize green and strong; without it the cobs stay small.
steps: Top-dress with urea when the soil is moist: a small pinch in a ring a hand-width from each plant.
Cover the fertilizer with soil.
Mix compost or well-rotted manure into the soil every season.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Angular leaf spot
conditions.headline: Your beans may have angular leaf spot
signs: Brown spots with straight edges that stop at the leaf veins
Spots appear after rain
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is making angular brown spots on the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: It spreads in wet weather and through seed, and can make leaves fall early.
steps: Pick off the worst leaves and remove them from the field.
Do not work in the field while the leaves are wet.
Next season, use clean seed and rotate with maize.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Bean rust
conditions.headline: Your beans may have bean rust
signs: Rusty powder under the leaves
Small raised spots that rub off on your finger
conditions.whatsHappening: A rust fungus is growing on the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: It spreads fast with wind and dew and can cut your harvest if it starts before flowering.
steps: Remove badly affected leaves.
Give plants space so air can move between them.
Next season, plant a rust-tolerant variety.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Anthracnose
conditions.headline: Your beans may have anthracnose
signs: Dark, sunken spots on pods
Dark lines along the leaf veins underneath
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is making dark sunken spots on the pods and leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: Infected seed carries it into next season.
steps: Remove affected plants and pods.
Do not keep seed from this field.
Rotate beans with maize or sorghum.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Bean common mosaic
conditions.headline: Your beans may have bean common mosaic
signs: Light and dark green patches on the leaves
Leaves curl downwards
conditions.whatsHappening: A virus is making a light and dark green pattern on the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: Aphids and infected seed spread it; sick plants give fewer pods.
steps: Pull out plants with strong symptoms.
Use certified seed next season.
Keep the field free of weeds.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Cassava bacterial blight
conditions.headline: Your cassava may have bacterial blight
signs: Angular brown spots between leaf veins
Yellow edges around the spots
Shoot tips drying out
conditions.notSeenHint: Sticky gum on stems — look for it
conditions.whatsHappening: Bacteria are making brown, angular spots on the leaves, and some shoots are drying from the tip.
conditions.whyItMatters: It spreads through cuttings, tools and rain splash. Left alone it moves across the field and cuts your harvest.
steps: Pull out plants with drying shoots and burn them away from the field.
Don’t take cuttings from this field for planting.
Clean your hoe and panga after working here.
Next season, plant clean cuttings of a resistant variety — your farmer promoter can help you find them.
sources: IITA cassava disease guidance
Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Cassava brown streak
conditions.headline: Your cassava may have brown streak disease
signs: Feathery yellow patches along the leaf veins
Brown streaks on green stems
conditions.notSeenHint: Brown, dry rot inside the roots — cut one open
conditions.whatsHappening: A virus is causing yellow patches on the leaves and can rot the roots.
conditions.whyItMatters: The roots can look fine outside but be spoiled inside, so the harvest is lost.
steps: Harvest affected plants early if the roots are big enough.
Don’t use cuttings from these plants.
Plant a tolerant variety from a trusted source next season.
sources: IITA cassava disease guidance
Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Cassava mosaic disease
conditions.headline: Your cassava may have mosaic disease
signs: Yellow and green patches on the leaves
Twisted, smaller leaves
conditions.whatsHappening: A virus spread by whiteflies and cuttings is twisting the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: Sick plants make fewer, smaller roots.
steps: Pull out plants with strong symptoms early.
Use cuttings only from healthy plants.
Plant a resistant variety next season.
sources: IITA cassava disease guidance
Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Cassava green mite
conditions.headline: Your cassava may have green mites
signs: Pale yellow speckles on young leaves
Small, bunched leaves at the tips
conditions.whatsHappening: Tiny mites are feeding on the young leaves, usually in dry weather.
conditions.whyItMatters: Heavy attacks slow growth until the rains return.
steps: Check the tips of a few plants each week.
Mulch to keep the soil moist.
Growth usually recovers when the rains come.
sources: IITA cassava disease guidance

conditions.name: Late blight
conditions.headline: Your potatoes may have late blight
signs: Dark, wet-looking patches on leaves
White mould under the leaves in the morning
conditions.whatsHappening: A fast-spreading fungus-like disease is killing leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: In cool, wet weather it can destroy a whole field in a week.
steps: Remove and bury badly affected plants today.
If you must spray, use only a product on RAB’s approved list from a registered agro-dealer. Follow the label, wear gloves and a mask, and keep children away.
Hill up soil around plants to protect the tubers.
Harvest only when the soil is dry.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Bacterial wilt
conditions.headline: Your potatoes may have bacterial wilt
signs: Plants wilt suddenly while the leaves are still green
Milky ooze from cut tubers
conditions.notSeenHint: Put a cut stem in water — milky threads mean wilt
conditions.whatsHappening: Bacteria in the soil are blocking water inside the plant.
conditions.whyItMatters: It stays in the soil for years and spreads with seed tubers and water.
steps: Pull out wilted plants with their tubers and bury them far from the field.
Don’t keep seed from this field.
Don’t plant potato, tomato or eggplant here for at least 2 seasons.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Early blight
conditions.headline: Your potatoes may have early blight
signs: Brown spots with rings like a target
Starts on older, lower leaves
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is making target-like spots on the older leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: It weakens the plant and makes tubers smaller.
steps: Remove the worst lower leaves.
Keep plants well fed with compost or manure.
Rotate potatoes with beans or maize.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Banana wilt (BXW)
conditions.headline: Your banana may have banana wilt
signs: Leaves turn yellow and wilt
Fruit ripens early and unevenly
Yellow ooze from cut stems
conditions.notSeenHint: Shrivelled male bud — check the bunch
conditions.whatsHappening: Bacteria are blocking the water inside the plant.
conditions.whyItMatters: It spreads fast on tools and through insects visiting the male flower.
steps: Cut down the sick plant and bury it on the spot.
Clean tools in fire or household bleach after each plant.
Remove male buds with a forked stick, not a knife.
Don’t move suckers from this field.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Black sigatoka
conditions.headline: Your banana may have black sigatoka
signs: Yellow-brown streaks on the leaves
Leaves dry out from the edges
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is making streaks and drying the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: Fewer green leaves means smaller bunches.
steps: Cut off badly affected leaves and use them as mulch away from the plants.
Keep the plantation open and weeded.
Feed plants with manure.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Late blight
conditions.headline: Your tomatoes may have late blight
signs: Dark, greasy patches on leaves and stems
Brown, firm patches on the fruit
conditions.notSeenHint: White mould under the leaves in the morning
conditions.whatsHappening: A fast-spreading fungus-like disease is killing leaves and fruit.
conditions.whyItMatters: In wet weather it can destroy the crop in days.
steps: Remove affected leaves and fruit today.
If you must spray, use only a product on RAB’s approved list from a registered agro-dealer. Follow the label, wear gloves and a mask, and keep children away.
Stake plants so leaves stay off the soil.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Tomato leaf miner (Tuta absoluta)
conditions.headline: Your tomatoes may have leaf miner
signs: Winding, see-through trails inside the leaves
Small holes in the fruit
conditions.whatsHappening: Small caterpillars are eating inside the leaves and fruit.
conditions.whyItMatters: They multiply quickly and can spoil most of the fruit.
steps: Pick off and destroy leaves with trails.
Remove damaged fruit.
Ask your agro-dealer about pheromone traps.
If you must spray, use only a product on RAB’s approved list from a registered agro-dealer. Follow the label, wear gloves and a mask, and keep children away.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Sweet potato virus disease
conditions.headline: Your sweet potato may have virus disease
signs: Small, twisted leaves
Pale or patchy colour on leaves
conditions.whatsHappening: Viruses spread by insects and vines are stunting the plants.
conditions.whyItMatters: Sick plants make few, small roots.
steps: Pull out plants with strong symptoms.
Plant vines only from healthy plants.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Sweet potato weevil
conditions.headline: Your sweet potato may have weevils
signs: Tunnels and holes in the roots
Small ant-like insects near the base
conditions.whatsHappening: Weevils are tunnelling into the roots through cracks in the soil.
conditions.whyItMatters: Damaged roots taste bitter and can’t be sold.
steps: Harvest mature roots now.
Hill up soil to cover cracks.
Destroy old vines and damaged roots after harvest.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Rice blast
conditions.headline: Your rice may have blast
signs: Diamond-shaped spots with grey centres
Broken, dark necks under the grain heads
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is making diamond-shaped spots on the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: If it reaches the neck of the grain heads, the grain stays empty.
steps: Don’t add more nitrogen fertilizer for now.
Keep the water level steady.
Ask your cooperative about a resistant variety.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Rice yellow mottle virus
conditions.headline: Your rice may have yellow mottle virus
signs: Yellow-orange mottling on leaves
Fewer tillers and short plants
conditions.whatsHappening: A virus is making the leaves mottled and the plants short.
conditions.whyItMatters: Infected fields give much less grain.
steps: Pull out sick plants early.
Remove volunteer rice and weeds around the field.
Plant a tolerant variety next season.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Coffee leaf rust
conditions.headline: Your coffee may have leaf rust
signs: Orange powder under the leaves
Pale yellow spots on the top of leaves
conditions.whatsHappening: A rust fungus is growing under the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: Trees lose leaves and give fewer cherries next season.
steps: Prune so air and light reach inside the tree.
Rake and bury fallen leaves.
If you must spray, use only a product on RAB’s approved list from a registered agro-dealer. Follow the label, wear gloves and a mask, and keep children away.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Coffee berry disease
conditions.headline: Your coffee may have berry disease
signs: Dark, sunken spots on green berries
Berries drop early
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is rotting the green berries.
conditions.whyItMatters: It can take a large part of the crop in wet seasons.
steps: Pick and bury infected berries.
Prune to open the tree.
If you must spray, use only a product on RAB’s approved list from a registered agro-dealer. Follow the label, wear gloves and a mask, and keep children away.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Antestia bug
conditions.headline: Your coffee may have antestia bugs
signs: Brown-orange shield bugs on berries and flowers
Blackened flowers and berries
conditions.notSeenHint: Potato-like taste in the brewed coffee
conditions.whatsHappening: Antestia bugs are feeding on the flowers and berries.
conditions.whyItMatters: They spoil beans and cause the potato taste that lowers coffee prices.
steps: Hand-pick bugs early in the morning.
Prune so the tree is open.
Tell your cooperative so it can plan control.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Sorghum anthracnose
conditions.headline: Your sorghum may have anthracnose
signs: Small red-purple spots on leaves
Spots join into long streaks
conditions.whatsHappening: A fungus is spotting the leaves.
conditions.whyItMatters: Heavy attacks reduce grain filling.
steps: Remove crop leftovers after harvest.
Rotate with beans.
Use clean seed of a tolerant variety.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

conditions.name: Striga (witchweed)
conditions.headline: Your sorghum may have striga
signs: Small weeds with purple flowers at the base
Sorghum stays short and pale
conditions.whatsHappening: Striga is a weed that attaches to the sorghum roots and steals water and food.
conditions.whyItMatters: Each plant makes thousands of seeds that stay in the soil for years.
steps: Pull striga by hand before it flowers, and burn it.
Add compost or manure to the field.
Rotate with beans or soybean.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

lowConfidence.headline: Inama is not sure what this is
lowConfidence.whatsHappening: The signs could fit more than one problem.
lowConfidence.whyItMatters: Different problems need different care. A wrong spray costs money and doesn’t help.
steps: Don’t spray yet.
Take a sharp photo of one sick leaf, close up, in daylight.
Send it to your farmer promoter or an agronomist to check.

healthy.headline: Your {crop} looks healthy
healthy.whatsHappening: Inama didn’t find signs of disease or pests in this photo.
healthy.whyItMatters: Checking early is how you catch problems while they are small.
steps: Keep checking a few plants each week.
Keep the field weeded.
Check again after heavy rain.

blurry.title: We couldn’t see the leaf clearly
blurry.body: The photo is too blurry to check. Nothing is lost — take one more.

dark.title: The photo is too dark
dark.body: Move into daylight or stand with the sun behind you, then take one more.

bright.title: The photo is too bright
bright.body: Shade the leaf with your hand or body, then take one more.

tips: Hold the phone a hand-width from one leaf.
Stand with the sun behind you, not in front.
Keep still for 2 seconds while the photo is taken.

questions.headline: This sounds like fall armyworm
questions.whatsHappening: Small holes in young maize leaves are often the first sign of fall armyworm feeding inside the funnel.
questions.whyItMatters: Maize this young can lose many leaves in a week.
steps: Walk your field in a W and look closely at 20 plants.
Crush egg clusters and small caterpillars by hand.

If 4 or more of the 20 plants have fresh damage: If you must spray, use only a product on RAB’s approved list from a registered agro-dealer. Follow the label, wear gloves and a mask, and keep children away.
questions.followUp: Add a photo so Inama can be surer.
sources: FAO guidance on fall armyworm management
Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Plant when the rains are steady
questions.whatsHappening: Seeds need moist soil for about two weeks after planting to come up well.
questions.whyItMatters: Planting too early risks seeds drying out; too late shortens the season.
steps: Plant after the soil is wet to about a hand’s depth.
Check the 7-day forecast on the Weather screen first.
Use certified seed from a registered agro-dealer.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Feed the soil at planting and when plants grow fast
questions.whatsHappening: Most crops need phosphorus at planting and nitrogen when they grow fastest.
questions.whyItMatters: Fertilizer at the wrong time or amount wastes money.
steps: At planting: DAP or compost in the planting hole, covered with soil.
For maize: top-dress urea at knee height, a small pinch per plant, then cover it.
Buy through Smart Nkunganire to get the subsidy price.
questions.followUp: Tell Inama your crop and field size for exact amounts.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Don’t spray before rain or in strong wind
questions.whatsHappening: Rain washes pesticide off the leaves, and wind carries it onto people and water.
questions.whyItMatters: Spraying at the wrong time wastes money and can harm your family.
steps: Spray only when no rain is expected for 6 hours.
Spray in the calm early morning.
Check the Weather screen for a “Go” on spraying.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Plant only clean cassava cuttings
questions.whatsHappening: Cassava diseases travel inside cuttings from sick plants.
questions.whyItMatters: Clean cuttings are the cheapest way to protect your next harvest.
steps: Take cuttings only from healthy plants without mosaic or brown spots.
Use a resistant variety — ask your farmer promoter where to find it.
Cut pieces about 25 cm long with 5–7 buds.
sources: IITA cassava disease guidance
Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Dry grain well, then store it airtight
questions.whatsHappening: Damp grain grows mould and attracts weevils.
questions.whyItMatters: Mould makes grain unsafe to eat and lowers the price.
steps: Dry until a grain cracks when you bite it.
Store in airtight (hermetic) bags, off the floor.
Check prices before selling — they often rise a few months after harvest.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Spots on bean leaves have a few causes
questions.whatsHappening: Brown spots can be angular leaf spot, rust or anthracnose.
questions.whyItMatters: Each needs different care, so it’s worth checking closely.
steps: Look under the leaves: rusty powder means rust.
Spots that stop at the veins suggest angular leaf spot.
Take a photo check so Inama can tell them apart.
questions.followUp: Add a photo so Inama can tell them apart.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Wilting bananas need action today
questions.whatsHappening: Yellow, wilting leaves can mean banana wilt, which spreads on tools.
questions.whyItMatters: One sick plant can infect a whole plantation.
steps: Cut down the sick plant and bury it on the spot.
Clean tools in fire or household bleach after each plant.
Remove male buds with a forked stick.
questions.followUp: Add a photo so Inama can be surer.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

questions.headline: Acidic soil needs lime before planting
questions.whatsHappening: Many hillside soils in Rwanda are acidic, which locks up nutrients.
questions.whyItMatters: Fertilizer works poorly in acidic soil.
steps: Ask your farmer promoter for a soil test.
Spread lime (ishwagara) about two months before planting.
Add compost or manure every season.
sources: Rwanda Agriculture Board (RAB) crop protection guidance

defaultAnswer.headline: Here is what Inama suggests
defaultAnswer.whatsHappening: Inama needs a little more detail to be sure.
defaultAnswer.whyItMatters: Advice is best when it fits your crop, field and season.
steps: Tell Inama which crop and field this is about.
If plants look sick, take a photo check.
For anything urgent, call your farmer promoter.
defaultAnswer.followUp: Add a photo or say which crop this is about.
